excerpt: Savannah's most crash-prone intersections and roads, what makes each dangerous, and your options if you are injured on one.
keyTakeaways: Savannah's 10 highest-crash intersections in 2023 — including I-16 at Dean Forest Road and Chatham Parkway and Abercorn Street at White Bluff Road — accounted for 428 of the city's 7,975 crashes, according to a Bike Walk Savannah analysis of GDOT data. Georgia's two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) govern how victims can recover compensation for injuries caused by red-light running, distracted driving, and poor road design across Chatham County.

faqs.question: What is the most dangerous intersection in Savannah, Georgia?
faqs.answer: No agency publishes an official ranking, but by crash count the I-16 interchanges at Dean Forest Road, Chatham Parkway and I-516 and Abercorn Street at White Bluff Road were among Savannah's highest-crash intersections in 2023, according to a Bike Walk Savannah analysis of Georgia DOT data. Other high-crash locations include Abercorn Street at East DeRenne Avenue and the Abercorn Street extension near Truman Parkway.

faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a car accident at a Savannah intersection?
faqs.answer: Call 911 to report the crash, seek immediate medical attention even if you feel fine, document the scene with photographs, exchange information with all involved drivers and witnesses, and contact a Savannah car accident lawyer before giving any recorded statements to insurance companies. Under Georgia law, the police report and your medical records become critical evidence in your injury claim.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident lawsuit in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, you have two years from the date of your accident to file a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia. Missing this statute of limitations deadline typically means losing your right to compensation.

faqs.question: Can I recover compensation if I was partially at fault for an intersection crash in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, which allows you to recover compensation as long as you are less than 50% at fault for the accident. However, your total award is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 20% at fault and your damages total $100,000, your recovery would be $80,000.

faqs.question: Why is Abercorn Street so dangerous in Savannah?
faqs.answer: Abercorn Street is one of Savannah's highest-crash corridors: it carries enormous traffic volumes through heavily commercialized areas with constant turning movements, driveway conflicts, and inadequate traffic infrastructure. Intersections along Abercorn — including White Bluff Road, East DeRenne Avenue and the stretch near Truman Parkway — were among the city's highest-crash locations in 2023, and all four of Savannah's red-light-camera intersections are on Abercorn (GDOT, 2024).

faqs.question: Can I sue the city if a dangerous road design caused my Savannah accident?
faqs.answer: Potentially, yes. If a government entity's failure to properly design, maintain, or signal an intersection contributed to your crash, you may have a claim against the City of Savannah or the Georgia Department of Transportation; Chatham County is largely immune from road-defect suits (O.C.G.A. § 36-1-4). These claims require written notice first — within 6 months for the City of Savannah (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5) and 12 months for Chatham County (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1) or the State (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26) — so consulting an attorney promptly is essential.
